group_assessment.weighting: Systematic-style qualitative review (databases to May 2024; 22 studies, 12 randomised trials) of macronutrient parenteral nutrition and Bayley or head-circumference outcomes in very preterm or very low birth weight infants. Class-level information on glucose and energy dose in neonates and the uncertain link between aggressive early parenteral nutrition and neurodevelopment. Not encephalopathic term infants, not a low-calorie regimen, not WWOX. The review's Conclusions pull in two directions (mandatory early nutrition; aggressive nutrition may not help).

entries.anchor: 2.2 Types of studies, participants and outcome measures

entries.proposition: Risk-of-bias judgments did not affect inclusion.
entries.snippet: The overall risk of bias judgments for each study did not affect their inclusion in this review.

entries.proposition: Of the 12 randomised trials, 7 had some concerns, 2 high risk and 3 low risk.
entries.snippet: The majority of studies (7 out of 12) were judged to have some concerns, while two studies were deemed to have an overall high risk of bias.

entries.proposition: The PRISMA diagram gives the identification, duplicate-removal, screening, full-text exclusion and inclusion numbers (22 studies included from 64 full texts).
entries.snippet: Visual attestation of Figure 1 (image nutrients-17-00232-g001): studies from databases n = 338; references removed n = 63; studies screened n = 275, excluded 211; assessed for eligibility n = 64, excluded 42 (language 2, outcomes 25, intervention 7, design 6, full text unavailable 2); included n = 22.

experimental_context.system: systematic review flow, preterm parenteral nutrition studies

entries.proposition: In the Stephens cohort, greater first-week protein and energy intake were associated with higher Bayley MDI at 18 months; this is an observational association.
entries.snippet: Higher Mental Development Index (MDI) scores on the Bayley scale emerged both for greater protein intake

entries.proposition: In the Morgan trial, the enriched regimen produced higher composite scores that were not statistically significant.
entries.snippet: although these results were not statistically significant

entries.proposition: The review writes that higher energy intake in an observational cohort 'can lead to hyperglycemia' that harms neurodevelopment at 24 months; the design is observational.
entries.snippet: showed how increased energy intakes (energy intake through PN ≥ 432 kcal/kg/week) can lead to hyperglycemia

entries.proposition: In the Bloomfield RCT extra amino acids did not change survival without neurological impairment but moderate-to-severe neurodisability was 16.5% versus 8.6% (adjusted relative risk 1.95).
entries.snippet: 27 out of 164 infants evaluated [16.5%] vs. 14 out of 163 [8.6%] in the placebo group

entries.proposition: Guideline glucose rates quoted for preterm infants are 4-8 mg/kg/min on day 1 rising to 8-10 mg/kg/min, with the stated need to avoid hyperglycaemia.
entries.snippet: The recommended glucose intake for preterm infants is 4–8 mg/kg/min (5.8–11.5 g/kg/day) on the first day of life, with a gradual increase to the target dose of 8–10 mg/kg/min (11.5–14.4 g/kg/day)

entries.proposition: The Conclusions state that adequate parenteral macronutrients are mandatory and may help neurodevelopment, and in the same paragraph that an aggressive approach may not correlate with favourable outcomes.
entries.snippet: We have learned that an aggressive approach to nutrition could lead to severe metabolic complications and may not correlate with favorable outcomes

entries.proposition: The review's own table states the carbohydrate neurological-outcome line as a need for tailored glucose to avoid hypo- and hyperglycaemia.
entries.snippet: Tailored glucose maintenance should be provided to avoid hypo/hyperglycemia

entries.proposition: Figures 2 and 3 give the risk-of-bias tables: RCT overall high for Blanco 2012 and Tan 2015, low for Thanhaeuser 2020, Gallini 2022 and Bloomfield 2022; Newcastle-Ottawa totals 7-9 for the nine cohort studies.
